title: How to Signal a Legal Fight Before You File One
documentTitle: Epic Games v. Apple — Exhibit F: Tim Sweeney Email to Apple Executives (July 17, 2020)
excerptForBlog: It's a sad state of affairs that Apple's senior executives would hand Epic's sincere request off to Apple's legal team to respond with such a self-righteous and self-serving screed -- only lawyers could pretend that Apple is protecting consumers by denying choice in payments and stores to owners of iOS devices. However, I do thank you for the prompt response and clear answer to my two specific requests. If Apple someday chooses to return to its roots building open platforms in which consumers have freedom to install software from sources of their choosing, and developers can reach consumers and do business directly without intermediation, then Epic will once again be an ardent supporter of Apple. Until then, Epic is in a state of substantial disagreement with Apple's policy and practices, and we will continue to pursue this, as we have done in the past to address other injustices in our industry.

lessonTitle: How to Signal a Legal Fight Before You File One
pullQuote: When a business dispute stops being about money and starts being about principle, the other side's lawyers are no longer the audience — the public and the courts are.
leadershipTraits: thinks in public records, not just private conversations
frames competitive disputes as structural, not personal
willing to absorb short-term loss for long-term leverage
situation: On July 17, 2020, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney emailed Apple executives after Apple's legal team responded to what Sweeney calls 'Epic's sincere request' — two specific asks that were denied. This short email is Epic's formal reply. The stakes are access to iOS consumers without paying Apple's platform fees or using Apple's payment system.
insight: Sweeney does something precise here. He doesn't argue the merits of his requests again. Instead, he reframes the entire dispute around a principle — 'open platforms,' 'freedom to install software,' 'no intermediation' — language that is much bigger than any single business negotiation. By invoking Apple's founding identity ('return to its roots'), he turns Apple's 'no' into a historical contradiction, not just a policy disagreement. That framing is useful in court, in press, and with regulators. The closing line — 'we will continue to pursue this, as we have done in the past to address other injustices' — signals that Epic is treating this as a campaign, not a one-time ask. This is classic platform strategy thinking: when you can't change the rules inside the platform, you go fight the rules from the outside.
application: If a platform, distributor, or gatekeeper denies a specific request, don't just move on. Before you close the conversation, state clearly — in writing — what principle the denial violates and what you intend to do next. This creates a record, signals resolve, and forces the other side to own their position publicly. Sweeney's email is three sentences of disagreement and one sentence of consequence. That ratio is worth copying.
